historical_claims.anchor: In January 1991, a set of underwater microphones near Ascension Island in the South Atlantic registered a sound that had begun near Heard Island in the southern Indian Ocean.
Its earliest arrival took about one hour, forty-four minutes, and seventeen seconds.
Researchers reported late reverberation for at least twenty-two minutes after the direct signal ended.
Sound travels through seawater at roughly fifteen hundred meters per second, more than four times its speed in air.
In 1944, Maurice Ewing and J. Lamar Worzel tested long-range sound propagation in the Atlantic.
Some of the transmissions were made at distances approaching nine hundred miles from the receiver.
A group in the Soviet Union made an independent discovery in the Sea of Japan in 1946.
The Navy established several SOFAR stations, but according to its own history they were never used as intended for that rescue system.
Aspects of the system were declassified in 1991, and scientists gained access to acoustic recordings that could also reveal earthquakes, submarine volcanoes, and marine animals.
On January thirty-first, the crew reported Beaufort force ten conditions and a wind instrument at its limit of sixty knots.
During the five days the sources operated, the experiment managed thirty-five long-distance transmissions.
The short experiment did not provide enough stable, identifiable travel paths to infer the ocean's temperature field as planned.
During the experiments of the later 1990s, researchers measured travel times over roughly three thousand to five thousand kilometers to precisions of a few tens of milliseconds.
A National Research Council review in 2000 did not give a simple all-clear.
In 2020, Wenbo Wu, Zhongwen Zhan, Shirui Peng, Sidao Ni, and Jörn Callies published an example using a roughly three-thousand-kilometer section of the eastern Indian Ocean.
In 2023, researchers extended the approach using hydrophones operated for the international nuclear-test monitoring system.

The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization operates eleven hydroacoustic stations to watch for evidence of nuclear explosions, including six deep-water hydrophone stations and five island stations that register sound energy converted into seismic vibrations.

claim_evidence.anchor: What holds sound near it is refraction.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: A sound-speed minimum acts as an acoustic waveguide through gradual ray refraction.

claim_evidence.anchor: a change in travel time can reveal a change in temperature averaged along an extended path.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: Acoustic travel times depend on the path-integrated sound speed; water temperature is a major contributor.

claim_evidence.anchor: In later accounts, the investigators were explicit: they had demonstrated extraordinary propagation, but they could not yet perform the intended oceanographic inversion from those measurements.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: HIFT established global reception but lacked stable recognizable arrivals for inversion.

claim_evidence.anchor: A short controlled signal and the continuous noise of traffic create different exposure patterns.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: Noise impact is a function of time, intensity, frequency and biological context.

claim_evidence.anchor: An undersea earthquake sends energy through the solid Earth. Some of it can enter the ocean and travel as acoustic waves.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: T waves can carry seismic energy in the sound channel.

claim_evidence.anchor: An earthquake has another: it happens without anyone needing to add another acoustic source to the sea.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: Author synthesis, grounded in the existing passive thermometry demonstration.
